per_company.ground_truth_answer: OMV Petrom integrates sustainability-related performance into Executive Board remuneration through a combination of Long-Term Incentive Plan (LTIP) and annual bonus mechanisms aligned with Strategy 2030. The LTIP focuses on sustainability targets with GHG emissions reduction target weighted at 25% and increase of women at management level at 10%. The 2024 annual bonus includes various Safety KPIs (zero work-related fatalities, Process Safety Event Rate, Total Recordable Injury Rate) with cumulated 15% weighting. The Remuneration Policy applies to both Executive Board and Supervisory Board since 2021, with an updated policy approved by the Ordinary General Meeting of Shareholders in April 2022 with 92% majority. The Supervisory Board remuneration is fixed (no variable sustainability-linked component). Climate-related consideration is based on the reduction of direct GHG emissions (Scope 1) and indirect GHG emissions from energy purchased (Scope 2) from operated and/or majority owned assets in 2024 against 2019 baseline.

evidence.text: The Executive Board remuneration at OMV Petrom consists of fixed and variable remuneration elements as well as benefits. The variable remuneration, which includes a Long-Term Incentive Plan (LTIP) and annual bonus, is aligned with the Strategy 2030 and places a strong emphasis on sustainability performance, including Environment, Social, Governance (ESG) related key performance indicators, such as carbon emission reduction.
evidence.source_section_header: DR GOV-3 Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes

evidence.text: In LTIP, the GHG emissions reduction target of OMV Petrom has a weight of 25%. Increase of the proportion of women at management level has a weight of 10%. Various Safety KPIs, including Zero-work related fatalities and Process Safety Event Rate and Total Recordable Injury Rate are included in the 2024 annual bonus scheme with a cumulated 15% weighting.
evidence.source_section_header: DR GOV-3 Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes

evidence.text: The Remuneration Policy in place applies to the Executive Board and Supervisory Board since 2021. The Supervisory Board remuneration is fixed. The definition of the climate-related consideration is based on the reduction of direct GHG emissions (Scope 1) and indirect GHG emissions from energy purchased (Scope 2) from operated and/or majority owned assets in 2024 against 2019.
evidence.source_section_header: DR GOV-3 Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: OMV Petrom provides explicit and comprehensive disclosure with specific quantifiable weightings (25% GHG in LTIP, 10% diversity in LTIP, 15% safety in annual bonus), clear metrics, governance framework, and shareholder approval details.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Repsol integrates sustainability-related performance into incentive schemes through a comprehensive multi-level framework. For the CEO, decarbonization and sustainability objectives represent 25% of annual variable remuneration, with specific targets including installed renewable generation capacity (5%), development of low-carbon platforms (10%), safety and fatalities/incidents index (5%), and talent/diversity objectives (5%). For all employees with annual variable remuneration, ESG objectives are integrated into individual and business unit targets with weighting between 20% and 45%. The Long-Term Incentive (LTI) for 2024-2027 affects all management staff, the CEO, and other employees, with 40% of objectives linked to the energy transition including Carbon Intensity Indicator reduction (20%), renewable generation capacity (10%), and renewable fuel production capacity (10%). Achievement scales are defined for each metric with minimum compliance thresholds and maximum levels at 100%. The Remuneration Policy was approved by the General Shareholders' Meeting in May 2023. Remuneration is reviewed annually by the Executive Committee, Remuneration Committee, and Board of Directors.

evidence.text: In the case of employees with annual variable remuneration, this remuneration is based on both the individual objectives of each employee and on the objectives of the business units. By 2024, objectives related to environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues have been integrated into all the objectives of each business unit, reaching a weight between 20% and 45%. In the particular case of the CEO, the weight of the objectives related to decarbonization and sustainability represents, in 2024, 25% of his annual variable remuneration.
evidence.source_section_header: Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes (GOV-3)

evidence.text: In addition, Repsol has implemented a Long-Term Incentive (LTI) for the period 2024-2027, which affects all management staff, including the CEO, and other employees, in which 40% of the objectives are linked to the energy transition. This LTI includes specific metrics such as the reduction of the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII), renewable generation capacity (GW) and renewable fuel production capacity (Mta).
evidence.source_section_header: Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes (ESRS 2 GOV-3)

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Repsol provides extensive and detailed disclosure with specific weightings for CEO (25% annual variable), employees (20-45%), and LTI (40% energy transition), specific measurable KPIs, achievement scales, governance processes, and coverage across all organizational levels.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: SBM Offshore integrates sustainability-related performance into Management Board incentive schemes through its Short-Term Incentive (STI) Program based on three sets of key performance indicators: Profitability, Growth, and Sustainability. Sustainability is one of three material performance areas in the STI. The Supervisory Board, upon recommendation of the Appointment and Remuneration Committee, determines target achievements for each performance measure. For 2024, nine performance indicators were established, with the Company's performance resulting in 126% of salary for the CEO and 94.5% for other Management Board members. Climate-related considerations are specifically factored into remuneration, with emission-related targets representing the short-term incentive component for the management board and employees. There are no performance targets for the Supervisory Board, which allows for an unmitigated focus on long-term value creation. The Supervisory Board may adjust the STI outcome down by 10%.

evidence.text: The Management Board remuneration policy includes a short-term incentive based on key performance indicators. One of the performance areas is sustainability performance. For each of the performance measures, the Supervisory Board, upon the recommendation of the Appointment and Remuneration Committee, determines the target achievement. There are no performance targets for the Supervisory Board, which allows for an unmitigated focus on long-term value creation.
evidence.source_section_header: Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes (ESRS 2 - GOV-3)

evidence.text: The Short-Term Incentive Program is based upon short-term operational performance, which includes three sets of performance indicators: Profitability; Growth; Sustainability. For 2024, a total of nine performance indicators were established. The Company's performance resulted in performance of 126% of salary for the CEO and 94.5% for the other Management Board member(s).
evidence.source_section_header: SHORT-TERM INCENTIVE PROGRAM OF THE MANAGEMENT BOARD

evidence.text: Climate-related considerations are factored into the remuneration of management according to the method explained in remuneration sections, in which emission-related targets represent the short-term incentive for the management board and employees.
evidence.source_section_header: Policies and Governance (Emissions)

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report clearly identifies sustainability as one of three STI performance areas, documents emission-related targets in compensation, shows actual 2024 outcomes, and distinguishes Management Board (variable) from Supervisory Board (no performance targets) treatment.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Shell integrates sustainability-related performance into remuneration schemes designed to support reducing operational emissions and helping customers reduce their emissions. The majority of employees participate in the annual bonus scheme, while Executive Directors and other nominated employees receive long-term share awards. The Remuneration Committee (REMCO) met five times during 2024 with sustainability-related matters relevant to remuneration being regularly addressed. Shell's climate-related targets and ambition are reflected in the remuneration of senior management and employees, with performance in the energy transition measured against these targets. The sustainability statement references the Directors' Remuneration Report (pages 188-190) for detailed metrics, performance conditions, and the proportion of variable remuneration dependent on sustainability-related performance, but does not disclose the specific metrics or weightings within the sustainability statement itself.

evidence.text: Our remuneration schemes are designed to support Shell in achieving its corporate strategy. We have established remuneration structures to support us in reducing our operational emissions and to support customers in reducing their emissions. The majority of employees participate in the annual bonus scheme. Executive Directors and other nominated employees receive long-term share awards.
evidence.source_section_header: Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes (GOV-3)

evidence.text: The Remuneration Committee (REMCO) met five times during 2024, with sustainability-related matters relevant to remuneration being regularly addressed. This section includes details of the schemes, including the sustainability-linked measures and targets and metrics used in the performance assessment, the proportion of variable remuneration dependent on sustainability-related performance.
evidence.source_section_header: Integration of sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes (GOV-3)

evidence.text: Shell's performance and progress in the energy transition is measured with respect to our climate-related targets and ambition, including those reflected in the remuneration of senior management and employees.
evidence.source_section_header: Progress in implementing the transition plan

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Shell confirms sustainability integration in remuneration and references specific mechanisms (annual bonus, long-term share awards, REMCO oversight), but the detailed quantification of sustainability-linked metrics and proportions is referenced to the Directors' Remuneration Report rather than fully disclosed in the sustainability statement itself.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Solvay integrates sustainability-related performance into three tiered incentive schemes: (1) Short-term incentive for Management, Senior Management, and Executives with sustainability accounting for 15% of total incentive weighting; (2) Global Profit Sharing for non-management employees with sustainability at 15%; (3) Long-term incentive for Senior Management and Executives with sustainability at 20%. All schemes are structured around performance pillars including financial performance and company sustainability ambition. Specific 2024 sustainability targets include GHG emissions reduction (Scope 1 & 2) to 7,170 kT CO2 eq, Safety (Recordable Injuries) target of 40, and Diversity (% women in mid and senior management) target of 27.3%. For ELT and Senior Management, GHG emission reduction targets are set in both STI and LTI plans. For general Management population, GHG reduction is part of the STI. GHG reduction is also reflected in the Profit Sharing plan for non-management employees. The target-setting process involves the Global Incentive Committee, Executive Leadership Team, Compensation Committee, and Board of Directors.

evidence.text: We operate different incentive schemes for different employee groups: Short-term incentive scheme: applicable to the Management, Senior Management, and Executive population, Global Profit Sharing scheme: applicable for non-management employees, and Long-term incentive scheme: applicable for Senior Management and Executives. All these schemes share the common objective of rewarding employees for achieving strategic company objectives.
evidence.source_section_header: GOV-3 Sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes

evidence.text: The sustainability-related targets account for: 15% of the Short-term incentive scheme for all management levels. 15% of the Global Profit Sharing scheme for non-management levels. 20% of the Long-term incentive scheme for all executives.
evidence.source_section_header: GOV-3 Sustainability-related performance in incentive schemes

evidence.text: For the ELT and the Senior Management - GHG emission reduction targets are set in both the Short-term Incentive plan as well as in the Long-term Incentive plan. For the general Management population the GHG emission reduction is part of the Short-term Incentive plan. GHG emission reduction is also reflected in the Company Profit Sharing plan applicable to the non-management employees.
evidence.source_section_header: E1 GOV-3 Integration of sustainability related performance in incentive schemes

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Solvay provides detailed disclosure with specific weightings (15-20%) across three incentive tiers, quantified sustainability targets, governance approval process, and comprehensive coverage from executives to non-management employees.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: TotalEnergies integrates sustainability-related performance into incentive and remuneration schemes through a multi-tiered approach. For the Chairman and CEO, annual variable compensation is 61% financial and 39% extra-financial criteria (safety, GHG emissions reduction, transition strategy supervision, renewables profitability, CSR performance). Since 2019, GHG emissions criteria have been included in the Chairman and CEO's variable compensation, and since 2020 climate-related conditions have been part of performance share plans. For the 2024 grant performance share plan specifically, climate-related award criteria account for 30% (15% lifecycle carbon intensity of energy products sold, 15% methane emissions changes). For senior executives, 30% of annual variable compensation is tied to extra-financial criteria including safety, GHG reduction, carbon intensity, and diversity. For all eligible employees (12,000+ beneficiaries in performance share plans), 30% of performance conditions are extra-financial focused on GHG reduction and carbon intensity. The compensation policy is reviewed annually by the Board of Directors on recommendation of the Compensation Committee.

evidence.text: In order to set a compensation aligned with the Company's performance, the variable portion of the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer's compensation takes into account both quantifiable targets (financial, Safety and GHG emission change parameters) and qualitative criteria (personal contribution). The Board of Directors decided, starting in 2019, to change the criteria for determining the variable portion of the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer's compensation, in particular by including a quantifiable criterion related to the change in GHG emissions (Scope 1+2) from operated facilities.
evidence.source_section_header: 5.1.2.3 Incentive mechanisms linked to sustainability performance (GOV-3)

evidence.text: For the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, annual variable compensation is predominantly linked to financial performance, which represents 61% of the total. Extra-financial criteria account for the remaining 39% and encompass safety performance, greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction, supervision of the transition strategy, profitability of renewables, and corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance. For senior executives, extra-financial criteria account for 30% of annual variable compensation.
evidence.source_section_header: 5.1.2.3 Incentive mechanisms linked to sustainability performance (GOV-3)

evidence.text: For the 2024 grant performance share plan, award criteria linked to climate objectives account for 30% (15% of the award is linked to a lifecycle carbon intensity criterion for energy products sold to the Company's customers, and 15% to a criterion linked to changes in methane emissions). The Board of Directors has a proactive approach to this issue. The compensation policy for the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer is reviewed annually by the Board of Directors, on the recommendation of the Compensation Committee.
evidence.source_section_header: 5.1.2.3 Incentive mechanisms linked to sustainability performance (GOV-3)

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: TotalEnergies provides highly detailed, quantified disclosure with specific weightings (39% CEO extra-financial, 30% for senior executives and performance share plans), identification of specific sustainability metrics, coverage across all organizational levels (12,000+ beneficiaries), and clear governance process.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Vopak integrates sustainability-related performance into remuneration incentives linked to key areas of sustainability performance. The targets linked to Vopak's strategic framework and sustainability roadmap have been translated into remuneration incentives based on four key metrics: Total Injury Rate (TIR), Process Safety Event Rate (PSER), gender diversity, and GHG emissions reduction. These targets are reviewed periodically to ensure alignment with the double materiality analysis. Board-level remuneration policies have been implemented aligned with GHG reduction goals, with the GHG emissions reduction metric being part of the Executive Board's (EB) short- and long-term incentive program. Detailed information on the incentive programs is referenced to the Remuneration report section of the Annual Report. The sustainability statement itself does not provide specific quantified weightings or percentages for the sustainability-linked components of variable remuneration.

evidence.text: The targets linked to Vopak's strategic framework and sustainability roadmap have been translated into remuneration incentives linked to key areas of sustainability performance and are explained in more detail in the Remuneration section.
evidence.source_section_header: Sustainability strategy and roadmap

evidence.text: These are based on: Total Injury Rate (TIR), Process Safety Event Rate (PSER), gender diversity, and GHG emissions reduction. These targets are reviewed periodically to ensure alignment with our double materiality analysis.
evidence.source_section_header: Sustainability strategy and roadmap

evidence.text: To encourage emissions reductions, we have implemented board-level remuneration policies aligned with our GHG reduction goals. Our GHG emissions reduction metric is part of the EB's short- and long-term incentive program and explained in detail in the Remuneration report.
evidence.source_section_header: Governance, policies, and standards

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Vopak identifies the four specific sustainability metrics integrated into remuneration (TIR, PSER, gender diversity, GHG reduction) and confirms board-level incentive alignment, but the detailed quantification (specific weightings, percentage of variable pay) is referenced to the separate Remuneration report rather than disclosed within the sustainability statement.

questions.question: Does the undertaking have a transition plan for climate change mitigation? If yes, is the transition plan aligned with the objective of limiting global warming to 1.5°C? If no transition plan exists, what is the undertaking's timeline for adopting one?

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Aker BP does NOT have a transition plan for climate change mitigation as defined by the ESRS. The company explicitly states: 'Aker BP does not have any targets to reduce our scope 3 emissions. As a result, we do not have a climate transition plan in line with the ESRS' requirements and do not have a timeline for if or when we will develop such a plan.' While the company has set Scope 1 and 2 emission reduction targets (50% by 2030 and near zero by 2050 compared to 2017 baseline), these targets are described as 'not science-based' and not aligned with the 1.5°C objective. The company does have a decarbonisation plan with operational emissions reduction measures (electrification, energy efficiency, CCS readiness), but this does not constitute a full ESRS-compliant transition plan due to the absence of Scope 3 targets.

evidence.source_section_header: E1-1 – Transition plan for climate change mitigation
evidence.text: Aker BP does not have any targets to reduce our scope 3 emissions. As a result, we do not have a climate transition plan in line with the ESRS’ requirements and do not have a timeline for if or when we will develop such a plan.

evidence.source_section_header: 2.4 Targets
evidence.text: We aim to reduce our operational control scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by 50 percent by 2030 compared with our 2017 baseline of 1.25 million t CO₂e. By 2050, we aim to achieve near-zero operational control and equity share scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions.

evidence.source_section_header: 2.4 Targets
evidence.text: Our climate-related targets are not science-based but are in line with national and international expectations for emission reductions in our industry.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Despite the absence of an ESRS-compliant transition plan, the disclosure quality is High because Aker BP transparently and comprehensively addresses both parts of the question: (1) it explicitly states it does NOT have a transition plan per ESRS requirements due to absence of Scope 3 targets, and (2) it clearly states its existing targets are not science-based. The candid acknowledgment of limitations, combined with detailed disclosure of existing Scope 1&2 measures and a 2017 baseline, constitutes thorough disclosure.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, BASF has a comprehensive transition plan for climate change mitigation that is explicitly aligned with the 1.5°C objective. BASF aims to reduce Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 25% by 2030 compared to 2018 and to achieve net zero emissions by 2050. The targets are aligned with the IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE) scenario, which is compatible with limiting global warming to 1.5°C. BASF plans to invest approximately €300 million in Scope 1 emission reduction measures and approximately €250 million in renewable energy supply between 2025 and 2028. Key decarbonization levers include electrification of steam crackers using renewable energy, use of CO2-free hydrogen, development of new low-emission production processes (e.g., methane pyrolysis, e-crackers), expansion of renewable electricity procurement, and carbon capture and storage. BASF has validated its Scope 1 and 2 targets through the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) as consistent with the 1.5°C pathway.

evidence.text: We want to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from our production processes (Scope 1) and our energy purchases (Scope 2) by 25% by 2030 compared to the base year of 2018, and are aiming to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.
It is compatible with limiting global warming to 1.5℃ based on the emission reduction pathways described by the International Energy Agency (IEA) in its study entitled "Net Zero by 2050."

The transition plan is embedded in our financial planning and was approved by the Board of Executive Directors and the Supervisory Board. It is based on investments of around €300 million in Scope 1 measures and €250 million in renewable energies between 2025 and 2028.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: BASF provides comprehensive disclosure with explicit 1.5°C alignment through IEA NZE scenario and SBTi validation. The transition plan includes specific targets, financial commitments, decarbonization levers, and timeline. Both parts of the question are fully addressed.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, Eni has a comprehensive transition plan called the 'Decarbonization Plan' that is aligned with the 1.5°C objective. The plan's pathway has been identified through actions from major international scenarios aimed at achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2050 to help keep the global temperature rise within 1.5°C by 2100, with reference to IPCC category C1 and IEA NZE scenarios. The structure of the pathway is described as 'substantially compatible with these scenarios.' The company targets Net Zero Carbon Footprint (Scope 1+2) for Upstream by 2030, for Eni overall by 2035, and Net Zero Lifecycle GHG emissions and Net Carbon Intensity (including Scope 3) by 2050. The plan includes investments in renewables, biorefining, carbon capture and storage, and energy efficiency.

evidence.source_section_header: Decarbonization Plan
evidence.text: The stages of this pathway have been identified through a prioritization exercise of the different actions, based on both internal analyses and the proposed actions from major international scenarios aimed at achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2050 to help keep the global temperature rise within 1.5℃ by 2100.

evidence.source_section_header: Decarbonization Plan
evidence.text: Eni has set a goal of net zero Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions for the Upstream sector by 2030 (Net Zero Carbon Footprint Usptream), and for the entire Eni group by 2035 (Net Zero Carbon Footprint Eni). Additionally, Eni has a goal of net zero Scope 1, 2, and 3 GHG emissions, related to the lifecycle of energy products sold by 2050, both in absolute terms

evidence.source_section_header: Decarbonization Plan
evidence.text: Even within comparative limits, the structure of this pathway, in terms of levers and emission reduction targets, is substantially compatible with these scenarios. For further information, see IPCC category C1 and IEA NZE scenarios, in the W Scenarios of the main international organizations, A Main GHG emission reduction targets, and A Decarbonization levers sections.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Eni provides comprehensive disclosure with alignment to 1.5°C through IPCC C1 scenarios and IEA NZE. The plan describes the pathway as 'substantially compatible' with these scenarios. It includes specific near-, medium-, and long-term targets across all scopes, detailed decarbonization strategies, and investment commitments.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, Equinor has a comprehensive Energy Transition Plan (ETP) that is aligned with the 1.5°C objective. Equinor aims to reduce its net operated (scope 1+2) emissions by 50% from 2015 to 2030, at a pace and scale described as consistent with a science-based, 1.5℃-aligned trajectory as defined by IPCC pathways. The company has a net-zero ambition for 2050. The ETP is aligned with the company's strategy and integrated into the business planning process. It was approved by the board of directors and the CEO. However, Equinor's ambitions have NOT been assessed by the Science Based Targets Initiative (SBTi), which currently does not have a sector-specific standard for the oil and gas industry.

evidence.source_section_header: E1-1 Transition plan for climate change mitigation
evidence.text: We aim to reduce our net operated (scope 1+2) emissions by 50% from 2015 to 2030, a pace and scale consistent with a science based, 1.5℃-aligned trajectory as defined by IPCC pathways'

evidence.source_section_header: E1-1 Transition plan for climate change mitigation
evidence.text: The plan sets out the ambitions and actions, in the short and medium term, to support our net-zero ambition for 2050.

evidence.source_section_header: E1-4 Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation
evidence.text: Our ambitions have not been assessed by the Science-Based Targets Initiative (SBTi), which currently does not have a sector specific standard for the oil and gas industry.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Equinor provides comprehensive disclosure with 1.5°C alignment through IPCC pathways. The plan includes specific targets, a net-zero ambition for 2050, and is embedded in the company strategy and approved by the board. Equinor transparently discloses that its targets have not been assessed by SBTi.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Galp is in the process of maturing its energy transition plan and has not yet published a formal transition plan. The company states it is 'maturing its energy transition plan' considering the evolution of its portfolio following the Mopane discovery in Namibia and lower execution of renewables projects. Galp estimates approximately 35% of gross capex planned for 2025-2026 will be allocated to low-carbon activities including energy efficiency, biofuels, green hydrogen, renewable electricity, and electric mobility. However, the report does NOT explicitly state alignment with the 1.5°C objective. The company is reassessing its emission reduction targets and follows a 'progressive and pragmatic approach' balancing low-carbon investments with secure and affordable energy supplies. Galp is marked as 'Not applicable' regarding exclusion from Paris-aligned Benchmarks.

evidence.source_section_header: Transition plan for climate change mitigation
evidence.text: While Galp continues to be invested in long-term sustainable value creation and decarbonisation, this requires a progressive and pragmatic approach, balancing continuous investments in low-carbon solutions with the need to maintain secure and affordable energy supplies, in line with strategy execution.

evidence.source_section_header: Transition plan for climate change mitigation
evidence.text: Galp is maturing its energy transition plan, considering as well the ongoing evolution of its portfolio following the recent potentially transformative Mopane discovery in Namibia and the lower execution of renewables projects. The Company will continue to follow market demand and regulatory developments in the energy transition space, while ensuring a disciplined execution of new projects and key investments. Galp estimates to publish its energy transition plan upon maturing its portfolio assessment and always ensuring alignment with disclosure requirements.

evidence.source_section_header: Transition plan for climate change mitigation
evidence.text: Galp foresees that c.35% of the gross capex planned for 2025-2026 will be allocated to low-carbon activities. The plan includes several projects that are either committed or at an advanced stage of development in energy efficiency, biofuels, green hydrogen, renewable electricity, electric mobility and other low-carbon activities.

evidence.source_section_header: Targets
evidence.text: As Galp matures its energy transition plan and decarbonisation efforts in light of the potential portfolio evolutions, the Company is reassessing its emission reduction targets to ensure ambitious but credible objectives.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Galp provides partial disclosure: a transition plan is being developed but not yet published. There is no explicit 1.5°C alignment statement. The company takes a 'progressive and pragmatic approach' and is reassessing targets. Capex allocation to low-carbon activities is disclosed but the overall plan lacks the completeness required for High fulfillment.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, Helleniq Energy has a transition plan called 'Vision 2025' (approved by the Board of Directors in December 2021). However, the transition plan is NOT fully aligned with limiting global warming to 1.5°C. The company explicitly states that 'the targets set are not fully compatible with limiting global warming to 1.5℃, as outlined in the Paris Agreement, however, they focus on reducing the carbon footprint and aim for climate neutrality by 2050.' Helleniq acknowledges that as an energy company with net revenue above 50% from oil & gas activities, it cannot set science-based targets since the SBTi technical paper for oil and gas has not been finalized. The company is excluded from EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks. Key transition initiatives include renewable energy expansion targeting 2 GW by 2030, energy efficiency projects, CCUS evaluation, biofuels production, green hydrogen, and electromobility infrastructure.

evidence.source_section_header: E1-1 - Transition Plan for Climate Change Mitigation
evidence.text: HELLENIQ ENERGY has set targets, as described in section E1-4 - Targets Related to Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation, that are fully aligned with United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals and the European Green Deal. So far energy companies that have net revenue above 50% from oil & gas activities cannot set a science-based target since the pertinent technical paper and guidance has not been finalized by the Science Based Targets initiative yet. The Group monitors diligently the Science-Based Targets initiative regarding the Oil and Gas activities. Once the methodology is finalized, it will be assessed. For now, the targets set are not fully compatible with limiting global warming to 1.5℃, as outlined in the Paris Agreement, however, they focus on reducing the carbon footprint and aim for climate neutrality by 2050.

evidence.source_section_header: E1-1 - Transition Plan for Climate Change Mitigation
evidence.text: HELLENIQ ENERGY is an energy company with significant oil & gas activity, as such is excluded from the EU Parisaligned Benchmarks, as specified in the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453, which includes provisions for climate change transition risks.

evidence.source_section_header: E1-1 - Transition Plan for Climate Change Mitigation
evidence.text: HELLENIQ ENERGY’s transformation plan is integrated into and aligned with the organization’s comprehensive business strategy (Vision 2025) and financial planning.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Helleniq provides a moderately comprehensive disclosure. The transition plan exists (Vision 2025) with Board approval and specific initiatives (2 GW RES by 2030, CCUS, biofuels). However, the company explicitly acknowledges non-alignment with 1.5°C and lacks specific quantified interim emission reduction targets for Scope 1, 2, and 3. The absence of SBTi validation and exclusion from Paris-aligned Benchmarks further limit the fulfillment level.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, MOL Group has a transition plan for climate change mitigation, disclosed for the first time in the 2024 sustainability statement. The plan was approved by the Sustainable Development Committee of the Board of Directors in February 2025 and by the Board in March 2025. However, the transition plan is explicitly NOT aligned with the 1.5°C objective. MOL states that 'assessment of the transition plan’s compatibility with a 1.5℃ pathway faces difficulties not just from the point of view of geographical limitations, but also industry-specific ones.' The company's 2030 targets (25% absolute Scope 1 and 2 reduction vs. 2019, 5% Scope 3 use-phase reduction vs. 2022) are below the SBTi cross-sector pathway of 42% by 2030. MOL targets net zero GHG emissions on all scopes by 2050 and plans to allocate 30-40% of total CAPEX to low-carbon projects between 2025 and 2030. The company is excluded from EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks.

evidence.source_section_header: Transition plan and decarbonization levers
evidence.text: Expanding on MOL Group’s Shape Tomorrow strategy, the company also discloses its transition plan for the first time in the 2024 sustainability statement. The transition plan was approved by the Sustainable Development Committee of the Board of Directors in February 2025. As part of the sustainability statement, it was also approved by the Board of Directors in March 2025, and by the Annual General Meeting in April 2025. The plan includes key milestones for 2030 and 2050 with the following targets: Decrease absolute gross Scope 1 and 2 GHG emission by 25% by 2030 compared to 2019, Decrease absolute gross Scope 3 GHG use-phase emissions of our sold energy products (Category 11: Use of sold products) by 5% by 2030 compared to 2022, Reach net zero GHG emissions on all Scopes by 2050, Allocate 30-40% of total CAPEX to low-carbon and sustainable business projects between 2025 and 2030.

evidence.source_section_header: Assumptions of transition plan and 1.5℃ alignment
evidence.text: Assessment of the transition plan’s compatibility with a 1.5℃ pathway faces difficulties not just from the point of view of geographical limitations, but also industry-specific ones. A widely accepted, oil and gas industry specific benchmark for a 1.5℃ compatible gross absolute GHG emission pathway is not yet available. MOL Group will assess the feasibility of adopting such a plan once the relevant guidelines and resources, primarily from the Science Based Target Initiative (SBTi), become available.

evidence.source_section_header: Assumptions of transition plan and 1.5℃ alignment
evidence.text: For the above reasons, MOL Group’s 2030 targets are below the SBTi’s cross-sector pathway, which suggests that gross Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions should be reduced by 42% by 2030 and 90% by 2050 from 2020 levels. Based on the Group’s activities, MOL Group is excluded from the EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: MOL provides a structured transition plan with clear targets and governance approvals. However, fulfillment is Medium because the company explicitly states non-alignment with 1.5°C pathways, targets are below SBTi cross-sector requirements, and the company defers full 1.5°C alignment assessment to future SBTi guidance availability.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, MOTOR OIL Group has a transition plan for climate change mitigation that is explicitly stated as aligned with the 1.5°C target. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, OMV has a comprehensive transition plan for climate change mitigation that is integral to its Strategy 2030. OMV's targets are approximated to the IEA's Sustainable Development Scenario (SDS) for 2030. The company plans to allocate 40-50% of approximately EUR 3.8 billion annual organic CAPEX (2024-2030) toward sustainable projects.

OMV’s targets are set at both absolute and intensity levels, with the ultimate goal of achieving net zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in Scopes 1, 2, and 3 by 2050. For Scopes 1 and 2, OMV is aiming for an absolute reduction of 30% by 2030 and 60% by 2040. For the defined categories in Scope 3, OMV is aiming for an absolute reduction of 20% by 2030 and of 50% by 2040.

evidence.source_section_header: Temperature Alignment of OMV 2030 Targets

At this stage, OMV is confident that its Scope 3 emission reduction targets for 2030 are compatible with limiting global warming to 1.5℃, while Scope 1 and 2 targets come close to the ambition of making a fair contribution.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, Repsol has a comprehensive transition plan for climate change mitigation aligned with the 1.5°C objective. The company has set intermediate targets of 55% reduction in direct emissions (Scope 1 and 2) by 2030 compared to 2016, and 20% reduction in total emissions (Scope 1, 2, and 3) by 2030 compared to 2018 baseline. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, SBM Offshore has a transition plan for climate change mitigation committed to achieving Net Zero by no later than 2050, including Scope 1, 2, and one category of Scope 3 (Downstream leased assets). per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, Shell has a transition plan for climate change mitigation embedded in its Energy Transition Strategy 2024 (ETS24), approved by 78% of shareholders. Shell explicitly supports the 1.5°C goal of the Paris Agreement and believes its Net Carbon Intensity (NCI) targets are aligned with this objective. Shell derived its NCI targets from IPCC Sixth Assessment Report 1.5°C scenarios, applying a methodology that excludes scenarios overly reliant on carbon removals or bioenergy. For Scope 3 Category 11 (oil products), Shell set an ambition to reduce customer emissions by 15-20% by 2030, which it claims is more ambitious than the median scenario and compatible with 1.5°C warming limits. The company aims to become a net-zero emissions energy business by 2050. Shell's capital investment and business plans cover a 10-year cycle including funding to deliver its 2030 targets.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, Solvay has a transition plan for climate change mitigation. However, the plan is explicitly NOT aligned with the 1.5°C objective. Solvay's targets are to become carbon neutral on GHG Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2050, and to reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 30% and Scope 3 focus categories by 20% by 2030 vs. 2021 baseline. While these targets are more ambitious than those validated by SBTi in March 2023, Solvay explicitly states they are 'not compatible with the objective of limiting global warming to 1.5℃ in line with the Paris Agreement.' The company is actively looking at how to accelerate delivery of projects to potentially align with a 1.5°C target. The decarbonization roadmap has been reviewed by the Board of Directors and includes Scope 1&2 levers (energy efficiency, fuel switching, electrification, CCS) and Scope 3 reduction in 5 key categories representing 90% of Scope 3 emissions. Solvay allocated approximately EUR 25 million in CAPEX in 2024 and plans EUR 30-35 million annually until 2030.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: TotalEnergies has a comprehensive transition strategy for climate change mitigation with a long-term ambition of carbon neutrality by 2050. However, the company explicitly acknowledges that its targets are NOT aligned with the 1.5°C objective. TotalEnergies states that 'current trends indicate that the evolution of the global energy mix is not compatible with limiting global warming to 1.5℃' and notes there is 'currently no consensus on GHG emission reduction targets or trajectories applicable at the scale of a company in a given sector and which would be compatible with a given global temperature target.' The company's investment criteria assess projects against the Paris Agreement's 'well below 2°C' objective (not 1.5°C). Its lifecycle carbon intensity targets (25% reduction by 2030) place it on a trajectory close to the IEA's Announced Pledges Scenario (APS), not the more stringent 1.5°C NZE pathway. TotalEnergies emphasizes a 'balanced transition strategy' maintaining oil and gas production and is excluded from EU Paris-aligned benchmarks.

evidence.source_section_header: How TotalEnergies' 2030 targets compare to the IEA scenarios

The "Stated Policies" scenario (STEPS) of the International Energy Agency provides an idea of the direction taken by the energy sector based on the most recent policies in countries around the world.

evidence.source_section_header: How TotalEnergies' 2030 targets compare to the IEA scenarios
evidence.text: From a scientific perspective, there are a multitude of transition scenarios and there is currently no consensus on GHG emission reduction targets or trajectories applicable at the scale of a company in a given sector and which would be compatible with a given global temperature target.

evidence.source_section_header: How TotalEnergies' 2030 targets compare to the IEA scenarios
evidence.text: Its targets for reducing the lifecycle carbon intensity of energy products sold(4) (a 17% reduction by 2025 and a 25% reduction by 2030) put TotalEnergies on a trajectory close to the Announced Pledges Scenario (APS) in the IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2023, which assumes that the States party to the Paris Agreement fulfill all their carbon neutrality objectives.

evidence.source_section_header: Exclusion of the Company from the "Paris Agreement" benchmarks
evidence.text: TotalEnergies is excluded from the EU Paris-aligned benchmark in accordance with the exclusion criteria stated in Articles 12(1)(d) to (g) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/1818, since it derives more than 10% of its revenues from the exploration, extraction, distribution or refining of liquid fuels.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: TotalEnergies provides comprehensive disclosure of its transition strategy with detailed targets, IEA scenario benchmarking, investment criteria, and explicit acknowledgment of non-alignment with 1.5°C. The transparency about both the transition plan and its limitations regarding 1.5°C alignment fully addresses both parts of the ESRS E1-1 question.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, Vopak has a transition plan for climate change mitigation, but it is explicitly NOT aligned with the objective of limiting global warming to 1.5°C. Vopak's plan targets net-zero emissions by 2050 with a mid-term target of 30% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by 2030 compared to 2021 baseline. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Aker BP's undertaking reports on pollutant emissions to air, water, and soil through its comprehensive Pollution section (E2). Emissions to air include NOx (2,213 tonnes/year), SOx (43 tonnes/year), and nmVOC (2,272 tonnes/year) from combustion of diesel and fuel gas on installations and drilling rigs. Pollution to water includes discharged produced water containing pollutants such as phenols, benzene, BTEX compounds, and metals (arsenic, cadmium, lead, zinc, naphthalene, and PAHs). The undertaking uses and discharges chemicals containing substances of concern (SOC) and substances of very high concern (SVHC). Specific SOC chemicals with health hazards include those causing carcinogenicity (H350/H351: 351 tonnes/year), reproductive toxicity (H360: 311 tonnes/year), respiratory sensitization (H334: 580 tonnes/year), and skin sensitisation (H317: 5,817 tonnes/year). SVHC identified include CAS 111-30-8 (258,533 kg used, 8,634 kg discharged) and CAS 625-45-6 (692 kg used, 415 kg discharged). Environmental management follows NORSOK S-003 standards and Norwegian discharge permits, with drinking water quality and soil not identified as material impacts given operations are located on the Norwegian continental shelf.

evidence.text: As all Aker BP's own operations are located on the Norwegian continental shelf (NCS), our activities leading to actual or potential pollution by emissions to air, discharges to sea as well as use and discharge of chemicals containing substances of concern or very high concern, are strictly regulated by Norwegian law and discharge permits. We acknowledge the environmental impact from our activities and our efforts to prevent, minimise and remediate the impacts, are anchored in our comprehensive environmental management system.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: BASF reports comprehensive pollutant emissions to air and water for 2024, excluding GHG. For air emissions, major pollutants include: nitrogen oxides (NO/NO2) at 7,596,114 kg/year, ammonia (NH3) at 1,894,780 kg/year, and nonmethane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs) at 2,622,097 kg/year. The company emphasizes safe handling through the TripleS sustainability steering method, REACH regulation compliance, safety data sheets in 40 languages, and the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) for classification and labeling.

Regarding substances of concern, SBM Offshore addresses hazardous materials management during decommissioning of FPSOs and other floating structures, including safe removal of hazardous materials. The company reports no oil spills above 1 barrel in 2024. Incidental environmental releases to air, water or land from offshore operations units are highly controlled and reported using the SBM Offshore Incident Management tool. However, the report marks ESRS E2-4 as not material for specific pollutant listing under the E-PRTR Regulation, and does not provide dedicated SVHC disclosures.

evidence.text: Emissions to air are an important determinant of local and regional air quality and can affect human health, flora and fauna or cultural heritage sites. The indicators used enable SBM Offshore to monitor the quantities in tonnes of non GHG emissions to the atmosphere from operations, including CO (Carbon Monoxide), NOx (Nitrogen Oxides), SO2 (Sulfur Dioxide) and VOCs (Volatile Organic Compounds).
evidence.source_section_header: Non-GHG emissions

evidence.text: Produced water is a volume liquid discharge generated during the production of oil and gas. After extraction, produced water is separated and treated (de-oiled) before discharge to surface water. The quality of produced water is most widely expressed in terms of its oil content. Limits are imposed on the concentration of oil in the effluent discharge stream or discharge is limited where reinjection back into the reservoir is permitted.
evidence.source_section_header: Oil in produced water discharges

evidence.text: During the projects, specialists inspect the assets to identify hazardous materials and to ensure the controlled removal and disposal of such materials as part of the decommissioning and recycling work. SBM Offshore aims to minimize adverse environmental and social impacts related to the decommissioning and recycling activities of each vessel, while maximizing circular economy opportunities.
evidence.source_section_header: Decommissioning and Recycling

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report provides specific quantitative data on pollutant emissions to air (CO, NOx, SO2, VOCs) and water discharges (oil in produced water), and mentions hazardous materials management. However, the report explicitly marks ESRS E2-4 as not material, lacks detailed E-PRTR Regulation Annex II pollutant data, and does not provide substance-of-concern or SVHC inventories.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Shell reports extensive pollutant emissions to air, water, and soil. Air emissions in 2024 include: Sulphur oxides (SOx) of 21 thousand tonnes, Nitrogen oxides (NOx) of 92 thousand tonnes, and Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) of 32 thousand tonnes. Additional air pollutants include benzene (201 tonnes), particulate matter (PM10: 3 thousand tonnes, PM2.5: 3 thousand tonnes), carbon monoxide (29 thousand tonnes), and metals including chromium (0.1 tonnes), copper (0.5 tonnes), and nickel (6 tonnes). Water discharges include total organic carbon (1,557 tonnes), metals such as arsenic (0.3 tonnes), cadmium (0.02 tonnes), chromium (0.3 tonnes), copper (0.3 tonnes), lead (0.1 tonnes), nickel (1 tonne), zinc (3 tonnes), and mercury (0.001 tonnes), along with nitrogen (340 tonnes) and phosphorus (63 tonnes). For substances of concern, Shell manages hazardous substances through its product stewardship approach, ensuring products such as fuels, lubricants and chemicals are safe throughout their life cycle. For assets with soil and groundwater contamination risk, Shell applies additional monitoring and control measures for benzene and ether oxygenates.

evidence.text: Emissions to air (operational control): Sulphur oxides (SOx) 21 thousand tonnes, Nitrogen oxides (NOx) 92 thousand tonnes, Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) 32 thousand tonnes, Benzene (C6H6) 201 tonnes, Particulate matter PM10 3 thousand tonnes, PM2.5 3 thousand tonnes, Carbon monoxide (CO) 29 thousand tonnes, Metals: Chromium (Cr) 0.1 tonnes, Copper (Cu) 0.5 tonnes, Nickel (Ni) 6 tonnes
evidence.source_section_header: Pollution of air, water and soil (E2-4) - Air quality

evidence.text: Pollutants discharged to surface water (operational control): Total organic carbon (TOC) 1,557 tonnes, Arsenic (As) 0.3 tonnes, Cadmium (Cd) 0.02 tonnes, Chromium (Cr) 0.3 tonnes, Copper (Cu) 0.3 tonnes, Lead (Pb) 0.1 tonnes, Nickel (Ni) 1 tonne, Zinc (Zn) 3 tonnes, Mercury (Hg) 0.001 tonnes, Nitrogen 340 tonnes, Phosphorus 63 tonnes
evidence.source_section_header: Pollution of air, water and soil (E2-4) - Water quality

evidence.text: Our products and operations involve the use of hazardous substances with the potential to harm people and the environment. We work to ensure our many products - such as fuels, lubricants and chemicals are safe throughout their life cycle. For sites where benzene or ether oxygenates are present or suspected, we apply additional monitoring, control and remediation measures.
evidence.source_section_header: Pollution (E2) - Product stewardship and Soil and groundwater

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report provides comprehensive quantified data on pollutant emissions to air and water with specific substances and amounts aligned with E-PRTR Regulation Annex II requirements. It addresses hazardous substances through product stewardship disclosures and references specific substances of concern (benzene, ether oxygenates). However, the report does not explicitly discuss SVHC under REACH.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Solvay reports consolidated pollutant emissions to air, water, and soil for 2024. Air emissions include ammonia (3,721,563 kg/a), carbon monoxide (43,578,491 kg/a), nitrogen oxides (3,101,161 kg/a), sulfur oxides (1,788,582 kg/a), non-methane volatile organic compounds (2,161,150 kg/a), particulate matter PM10 (194,299 kg/a), benzene (68,432 kg/a), and other pollutants including cadmium, naphthalene, and ozone-depleting substances. Water emissions include metals and compounds (arsenic, cadmium, chromium, copper, lead, mercury, nickel, zinc), nutrients (total nitrogen 1,785,321 kg/a, total phosphorus 99,974 kg/a), and organic compounds. No emissions to soil occurred under normal operating conditions in 2024. Regarding substances of concern and very high concern (SVHC): 5.3% of net sales involve marketed products containing substances of concern (SoC); 0.3% involve SVHC; and 4.7% involve Solvay Substances Risk Monitoring substances. In 2024, 26 black/red S-SRM substances were present in marketed products above 0.1% w/w concentration; 8,243 metric tons of Category 1 SoC (including SVHC) were marketed as products. Solvay uses a 0.1% w/w threshold for SoC identification aligned with REACH regulation, and is committed to phasing out SVHC and S-SRM substances from products.

evidence.text: The emissions data presented in this report represent a group-level consolidation of values from sites that exceed the specific thresholds established in Annex II of the E-PRTR Regulation. These thresholds are defined for each pollutant and environmental medium (air, water). In accordance with E-PRTR requirements, only emissions from sites surpassing these predetermined thresholds are included in the reported figures.
evidence.source_section_header: E2-4 Consolidated amounts of each pollutant (Pollution of air, water, and soil)

evidence.text: Solvay's industrial activities do not generate emissions to soil under normal operating conditions. Any emissions to soil would be due to uncontained accidental events (leaks, chemical spills, etc.). In 2024, no such events occurred; therefore, no emissions to soil need to be reported.
evidence.source_section_header: Soil Pollution Data

evidence.text: Solvay decided to use the threshold value of 0.1% w/w for SoC as it is referenced in the REACH regulation for EU Substances of Very High Concern (SVHC). Marketed products that are or that contain substances of concern (SOC): 5.3%; Marketed products that are or that contain substances of very high concern (SVHC): 0.3%; Solvay - Substances Risk Monitoring (S-SRM): 4.7%.
evidence.source_section_header: E2-5 Substances of Concern and Substances of very high concern - Marketed products

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report provides comprehensive disclosure with consolidated pollutant emissions data across air, water, and soil mediums, including specific quantities. SVHC and SoC are well-addressed with quantitative data on marketed products, including hazard class breakdowns and S-SRM monitoring. The company demonstrates methodological rigor by citing E-PRTR compliance and REACH regulation thresholds.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: TotalEnergies identifies families of pollutants specific to its activities including gaseous pollutants (SO2, NOX, NMVOC, PM) and aqueous effluents (nitrogen, heavy metals, BTEX, Hydrocarbons). In 2024, the company emitted: SO2 16,000 t/year, CO 12,000 t/year, NMVOC 35,000 t/year, NOx 57,000 t/year, PM 3,000 t/year to air; and TOC/COD 15,000 t/year, Total nitrogen 8,000 t/year, Total phosphorus 70 t/year, PAHs 4 t/year to water. For soil, the company does not conduct deliberate releases but manages accidental spills. Regarding substances of concern (SoC) and substances of very high concern (SVHC), TotalEnergies' European operated sites maintain updated lists of SoC and SVHC present in purchases and sales. The company aims to replace and minimize SoC use and phase out SVHC in its operations. For microplastics, the estimated release during polymer production and transport is approximately 0.0001% of total polymer production, with certification targets for Operation Clean Sweep by end 2025.

evidence.text: These families of pollutants contain gaseous pollutants (SO2, NOX, NMVOC, PM) and pollutants more commonly present in aqueous effluents (nitrogen, heavy metals, BTEX, Hydrocarbons). The Company does not carry out deliberate releases to soil although risks of soil contamination linked to the activities carried out by TotalEnergies may come from mainly accidental spills.
evidence.source_section_header: 5.2.2 Pollution - Management of Pollution

evidence.text: In 2024, the following quantities of pollutants were emitted by the operated sites: Sulfur oxide/dioxide (SO/SO2) into the air 16,000 t/year; Carbon monoxide (CO) into the air 12,000 t/year; Non-methane volatile organic carbon (NMVOC) into the air 35,000 t/year; Nitrogen oxide/dioxide (NO2/NO2) into the air 57,000 t/year; Dust (PM) into the air 3,000 t/year; Total Organic Carbon (TOC) or Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD)/3 in water 15,000 t/year; Total nitrogen (N, TKN) into water 8,000 t/year; Total phosphorus (P) into water 70 t/year; Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) into water 4 t/year.
evidence.source_section_header: 5.2.2.3 Quantitative data on substance releases to water, air and soil (E2-4)

evidence.text: TotalEnergies fully shares the desire to replace and/or minimize the use of substances of concern and to phase out the use of substances of very high concern in the industry. The Company regularly monitors product safety in order to eliminate and/or replace, where possible, substances of concern and extremely high concern that may be present in its industrial processes. In Europe, in accordance with the regulations, the Company's operated sites maintain an up-to-date list of substances of concern (Substances of Concern - SoC) and substances of very high concern (Substances of Very High Concern - SVHC) present in their purchases and sales.
evidence.source_section_header: 5.2.2 Pollution and 5.2.2.4 E2-5 Category Substances

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report comprehensively addresses E2-4 with specific quantitative data on pollutant emissions to air and water, identifies pollutant families, and addresses SoC and SVHC management. The only gap is limited quantification of SoC/SVHC substances (mentioned for Europe only), but overall disclosure is substantially complete.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Vopak's undertaking releases pollutant emissions to air, with the primary pollutants of concern being volatile organic compounds (VOCs), carbon dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, and benzene. According to Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 166/2006 (E-PRTR regulation), the company reported the following emissions to air in 2024: carbon dioxide (122,533 metric tons), nitrogen dioxide (323.75 metric tons), and benzene (178 metric tons). VOC emissions originate from storage tanks, loading and unloading operations, and vessel operations. Regarding substances of very high concern (SVHC), Vopak acknowledges that it is not currently able to fully disclose the share of net revenue derived from products and services containing SVHC and substances of concern (SoC) due to complexity in tracking and quantifying these substances across its product portfolio, as permitted by ESRS phase-in allowance.

evidence.text: For Vopak, the only Annex II pollutants of exceedance are carbon dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, and benzene. More precisely, the release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere was 122,533 metric tons, of nitrogen dioxide 323.75 metric tons, and of benzene 178 metric tons.
evidence.source_section_header: Note 1. Emissions to air

evidence.text: Negative impact Vopak's operations including chemical storage, handling, and vessel activities can lead to the emission of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). These compounds have a harmful impact on human health and the environment, contributing to ground-level ozone and particulate matter. These pollutants are known to cause respiratory issues and aggravate conditions like asthma.
evidence.source_section_header: Note 1. Emissions to air - Mapping of material topics with ESRS and attributed impact, risks, and opportunities

evidence.text: Vopak is not currently able to disclose the share of net revenue derived from products and services containing SVHC and SoC, as permitted by the ESRS phase in allowance. This is due to the complexity of tracking and quantifying these substances across our product portfolio and the challenges of obtaining consistent and detailed data.
evidence.source_section_header: Note 1. Emissions to air

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report provides specific quantitative data on air pollutant emissions under E-PRTR Annex II (CO2, NO2, benzene) and describes VOC emissions sources and impacts. However, fulfillment is Medium because the report lacks comprehensive emission data for water and soil pollution, and SVHC/SoC disclosure is explicitly deferred with phase-in allowance rather than fully disclosed.

questions.question: What is the undertaking's total water consumption, and how much of that consumption occurs in areas of high water stress?

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Aker BP does not disclose total water consumption or water consumption in areas of high water stress. The company states that water and marine resources are not a material topic for its own operations, which are located on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS), and that none of its own operations are in water-stressed environments. While the company acknowledges that water consumption may be material in parts of its upstream and downstream value chain due to construction activity abroad, it explicitly states that it has not yet obtained the necessary data and insight, and therefore has no related policies, actions, targets, or metrics to report under E3-4.

evidence.text: Aker BP's own operations are located on the NCS. We do not withdraw water from areas in waterstressed regions and none of our own operations are in water-stressed environments. The use of natural resources, such as water, is assessed as part of the DMA process. Water is not considered a material topic for Aker BP in our own operations.
evidence.source_section_header: 1.5.3.3 E3 - Water and marine resources

evidence.text: Water and marine resources are not a material topic for Aker BP's own operations. We have identified one material impact within this topic, as we believe that water consumption in our value chain could potentially prove to be material. As we have not yet been able to obtain the necessary data and insight into our value chain related to water and marine resources, we do not have any related policies, actions, targets or metrics to report.
evidence.source_section_header: 4 Water and marine resources

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report provides no quantitative water consumption data and no water stress area analysis. The company explicitly states it cannot report metrics for E3-4 as water is not material for own operations and value chain data is not yet available.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: BASF reports total water consumption of 76 million cubic meters in 2024. Water consumption at sites located in water stress areas (approximately 30% of production sites) amounted to 9 million cubic meters, while consumption at sites in areas of high or extremely high overall water risk (23% of production sites) was 6 million cubic meters. Water consumption is defined as the amount of water not discharged back into a water body, primarily attributable to evaporation in recirculating cooling systems. BASF also reports total water abstraction of 1,507 million cubic meters, total water use of 7,102 million cubic meters, and total recycled and reused water of 5,734 million cubic meters. BASF's water intensity was 1,171 cubic meters per million EUR of net revenue. Water stress areas are identified using the World Resources Institute's Water Risk Atlas.

evidence.text: Water consumption totaled 76 million cubic meters in 2024... Water consumption at BASF sites in water stress areas amounted to 9 million cubic meters. Water consumption at BASF sites in areas of high or extremely high overall water risk amounted to 6 million cubic meters.
evidence.source_section_header: Water balance of the BASF Group in 2024

evidence.text: Our water consumption is low compared with the total water volume sourced and therefore not a material topic for BASF in terms of the double materiality assessment.
evidence.source_section_header: E3-3 Global target

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report provides comprehensive quantitative data on total water consumption, water consumption in both water stress areas and high/extremely high water risk areas, water intensity, and recycled water volumes. The methodology for identifying water stress areas (WRI Water Risk Atlas) is also disclosed.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Eni reports total water consumption of 45 Mm³ (megalitres/million cubic meters) for operated activities and 9 Mm³ for consolidated not-operated activities in 2024, totaling approximately 54 Mm³. Of this, 17 Mm³ (operated) and 7 Mm³ (consolidated not-operated) occurred in areas of water stress, totaling 24 Mm³ or approximately 44% of total consumption. The company also reports 1,133 Mm³ of recycled and reused fresh water (90% fresh water reuse rate), total water withdrawals of 1,162 Mm³ (of which 89% is seawater), and 51% produced water reinjection rate. Eni has declared an ambition to achieve water positivity by 2050 at operated sites, with an intermediate target of water positivity by 2035 in at least 30% of sites with significant fresh water withdrawals in water-stressed areas.

evidence.text: Water consumption: 45 Mm³ (operated), 9 Mm³ (consolidated not operated). Water consumption in area with water stress: 17 Mm³ (operated), 7 Mm³ (consolidated not operated). Reused and recycled fresh water: 1,133 Mm³.
evidence.source_section_header: Water Consumption

evidence.text: About half of total expenditure for water resource management allocated to interventions at water-stressed area sites. Eni declared ambition to achieve water positivity by 2050 in operated sites.
evidence.source_section_header: Material Impacts, Risks and Opportunities / Targets and Commitments

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report provides detailed quantitative data on total water consumption, consumption in water stress areas (both operated and non-operated), recycled water volumes, reuse rates, and a breakdown by water source. Targets for water positivity are also included alongside methodological definitions.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Equinor does not disclose total water consumption or water consumption in areas of high water stress under ESRS E3-4. The company explicitly states that water and marine resources (ESRS E3) was not deemed material based on its double materiality assessment, which considered absolute water consumption and withdrawal data as well as expert input. The materiality assessment concluded that water is material to Equinor through the pollution and biodiversity standards rather than through water consumption and withdrawal. Equinor directs readers to its Sustainability data hub on equinor.com for consumption and withdrawal data.

evidence.text: Based on absolute water consumption and withdrawal data as well as the input from subject matter experts, "Water and marine resources" was not deemed material for Equinor. Instead, the materiality assessment revealed that water is material to Equinor through the pollution and biodiversity standards rather than water consumption and withdrawal. For more information on consumption and withdrawal please see the Sustainability data hub on Equinor.com (sustainability.equinor.com).
evidence.source_section_header: ESRS E3 - Water and marine resources

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report provides no quantitative water consumption data or water stress analysis. ESRS E3 was determined to be non-material and therefore E3-4 disclosures are omitted entirely. The company refers readers to external sources for this data.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Galp reports total water consumption of 3,198 thousand cubic meters (3.198 million m³) in 2024, up from 3,017 thousand m³ in 2023. Of this total, 3,036 thousand cubic meters occurred in water stress areas, representing approximately 94.9% of total consumption. Total water withdrawal was 7,941 thousand m³, with 7,657 thousand m³ from water stress areas. Total water discharge was 4,743 thousand m³. Total water recycled and reused was 1,515 thousand m³ (up from 1,112 thousand m³ in 2023). Water intensity was 912 m³/€M. In 2024, over 63% of Galp's operated sites were in areas experiencing water stress, and 35% were in areas with high or extremely high overall water risks, largely attributable to their location in Iberia. The Sines refinery was identified as a priority hotspot.

evidence.source_section_header: Operations in water stress areas in own operations

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: The report provides comprehensive quantitative data on total water consumption, consumption in water stress areas, water withdrawal, discharge, recycling, and intensity. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Helleniq Energy reports total water consumption of 8,468,614 m³ in 2024 (comprising 8,241,409 m³ from Hellenic Petroleum R.S.S.O.P.P. S.A. and 227,205 m³ from subsidiaries), an increase of 23% from 6,894,270 m³ in 2023. Total water discharge was 7,229,408 m³, with over 96% discharged to sea after treatment. The increase in water consumption was mainly due to increased fresh water consumption for fire protection at the Aspropyrgos refinery.

evidence.text: 98% of the total water consumed occurs in HELLENIQ ENERGY facilities located in Greece, which is characterized as one of the water stress areas according to WRI assessment.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: MOL Group reports total water consumption of 21,544 thousand m³ in 2024. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Motor Oil Group reports total water consumption of 657,286 m³ in 2024. per_company.ground_truth_answer: OMV reports total water consumption of 68,126,854 m³ in 2024 (down from 70,614,415 m³ in 2023). questions.question: What are the undertaking's operational sites located in or near biodiversity-sensitive areas, and what measures has it taken to avoid or minimize adverse impacts on ecosystems?

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Aker BP's production assets in its own operations are located outside biodiversity-sensitive areas. However, in 2024, Aker BP as a partner engaged in two non-operated exploration drilling operations in biodiversity-sensitive areas (SVOs - nationally designated areas). The Falstaff well (20% equity) is located approximately six kilometres within the outer border of the SVO Tobisfeltet 'Inner Shoal' in the North Sea, designated for vital habitats and breeding grounds for sand eels. The Elgol well (20% equity) is located approximately 17 kilometres northeast of the Goliat FPSO within the SVO Kystsonen Finnmark in the Barents Sea, a biodiverse coastal area. Additionally, two onshore power stations supplying offshore installations are located near biodiversity-sensitive areas: Johan Sverdrup's power station at Haugsneset lies within one km of the Gåsholmen and Årvikholmen nature reserve (IUCN IA) for seabirds, and Valhall's power converter station is within one km of the Røyrtjønn nature reserve (IUCN IA), a Ramsar-listed wetland. To minimize adverse impacts, Aker BP adheres to a mitigation hierarchy prioritizing avoidance, mitigation, restoration, and compensation. Mitigation measures for the Falstaff well included seabed surveys, timing drilling activities during spawning vulnerability periods, and collecting drill cuttings to prevent habitat disruption. For the Elgol well, operations were timed to avoid drilling during vulnerable biological resource lifecycle stages. Regular environmental monitoring shows no measurable negative impacts on sensitive areas from onshore power station activities. Aker BP has not implemented local impact mitigation measures for the onshore sites as no adverse impacts have been identified.

evidence.text: Production assets in Aker BP's own operations are located outside biodiversity-sensitive areas. In 2024, Aker BP as a partner engaged in two exploration drilling operations in biodiversity-sensitive areas, also known as SVOs. These operations were thoroughly risk-assessed in terms of potential impacts and planned to avoid any disruptive activities while ensuring adequate oversight.

evidence.text: Falstaff is located approximately six kilometres within the outer border of the SVO Tobisfeltet 'Inner Shoal' in the southern part of the North Sea. This area is designated as SVO due to its vital habitats and breeding grounds for sand eels. Preparations for Falstaff drilling have involved several surveys to assess seabed conditions and map important biodiversity features. The timing of the drilling activities was planned in accordance with the provisions of the Norwegian management plan for marine areas to avoid interference with sand eels' spawning and early life stages when they are most vulnerable. The drill cuttings generated during drilling were collected and sent ashore for further treatment to prevent physical disruption of sand eels' bottom habitats from discharges.

Valhall's onshore power converter station is located within one km of the Røyrtjønn nature reserve (IUCN IA), part of the Ramsar-listed wetlands that provide important breeding and wintering grounds for various bird species.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Aker BP provides comprehensive disclosure of its operational sites in relation to biodiversity-sensitive areas with detailed location-specific information, identification of biodiversity values, specific mitigation measures (seabed surveys, timing of activities, cuttings collection), and monitoring outcomes showing no measurable negative impacts. The mitigation hierarchy is clearly embedded in the company's biodiversity policy.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: BASF has systematically identified and assessed its operational sites in relation to biodiversity-sensitive areas since 2013, using the Integrated Biodiversity Assessment Tool (IBAT) and the Biodiversity Risk Filter (BRF) of WWF. In 2024, the assessment was expanded to include IUCN classifications (I, II, III), Ramsar wetlands, UNESCO Natural World Heritage Sites, Natura 2000 areas, and Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs). Nearly 15% of BASF's production sites are located in proximity to nature reserves or biodiversity-sensitive areas. No sites reported negative impacts on biodiversity-sensitive areas in 2024. To minimize adverse impacts, BASF employs the mitigation hierarchy approach: avoiding impacts, reducing impacts, supporting restoration, and contributing to value chain transformation. Key measures include implementing the Responsible Care Management System for environmental protection, establishing water protection concepts at all production sites, conducting regular environmental audits, steering the product portfolio toward sustainability via TripleS methodology, and responsible sourcing of renewable raw materials with biodiversity criteria and certification standards (RSPO, ISCC, REDcert). BASF also uses the STAR (Species, Threat, Abatement and Restoration) tool based on the IUCN Red List within a 10km radius of production sites. The company does not have dedicated biodiversity protection policies for site proximity but relies on its comprehensive Responsible Care Management System. A Nature Advisory Council comprising five independent experts provides guidance on biodiversity protection.

evidence.text: All BASF production sites in proximity to nature reserves must document potential direct negative impacts on biodiversity-sensitive areas. No such impact was reported by any site for 2024. Since 2013, we have been analyzing production sites in terms of their proximity to nature reserves, including with the help of the Integrated Biodiversity Assessment Tool (IBAT). In 2024, our assessment was expanded and now includes nature reserves pursuant to the classification of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) I, II and III as well as Ramsar, UNESCO Natural World Heritage Sites, Natura 2000 and Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs).

Using the STAR (Species, Threat, Abatement and Restoration) tool, we also calculated the STAR values for our production sites based on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. This analysis covered the sites themselves and a radius of ten kilometers.

evidence.text: We do not have dedicated policies for the protection of biodiversity in proximity to our sites, but instead use our comprehensive Responsible Care Management System. Alongside global requirements and health and safety standards, this also covers environmental protection. We have defined our global standards for emissions to air and water in Group-wide requirements.
