The company acknowledges lacking dedicated biodiversity-specific policies but relies on comprehensive environmental management systems.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Eni operates 32 concessions in the upstream Oil & Gas portfolio (approximately 655.5k hectares) and 28 operational sites (approximately 3.8k hectares) that overlap with priority biodiversity conservation areas including protected areas, Natura 2000 sites, and Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs). Additionally, 41 concessions and 62 sites are adjacent to such areas. Key operational sites with significant biodiversity impacts include: Val D'Agri (Italy) overlapping with a national park and 11 Natura 2000 sites with 154 hectares restored; Collarmele Wind Farm (Italy) overlapping with Natura 2000 and KBA areas with detection cameras and acoustic deterrents; Alaska Nikaitchuq/Oooguruk overlapping with Beaufort Sea Nearshore KBA with 5.4 hectares of tundra restoration; Ghana Cape Three Point overlapping with Amansuri wetlands KBA pursuing 'No Net Loss' with 11 hectares restoration and 22 hectares conservation offset; UK Liverpool Bay impacting a Ramsar site with dune restoration since 1994 and species reintroduction; and Spain Bonete Solar overlapping with Natura 2000 and KBA with vegetation management and habitat monitoring. To avoid and minimize impacts, Eni employs a mitigation hierarchy prioritizing prevention over correction, conducts Environmental Impact Assessments, implements site-specific Biodiversity Action Plans (BAPs), and applies the 'No Net Loss' principle. The company has adopted a No-Go Commitment not to operate in UNESCO World Heritage Sites and follows the BES Management Model to assess biodiversity loss risk.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Equinor operates 26 assets in protected areas (113,186 ha) and 36 assets in Key Biodiversity Areas/SVO (71,923 ha), with additional assets near sensitive areas (19 near protected areas covering 147,121 ha; 20 near KBA/SVO covering 78,846 ha). Two material sites are identified where avoidance and minimisation measures alone are insufficient: Dudgeon and Sheringham Shoal Offshore Wind Farms, which pose collision risks for key seabird species in North Norfolk Coast and Flamborough/Filey Coast SPAs. To minimize adverse impacts, Equinor applies a mitigation hierarchy through comprehensive site screening using GIS analysis with global biodiversity data (WDPA, KBA, SVO datasets), baseline surveys, environmental impact assessments, and stakeholder engagement. Measures include site-specific inventories mapping key biodiversity features, net-positive impact (NPI) plans for new projects in protected/sensitive areas, application of best available techniques (BAT), monitoring and research with IUCN, IOC-UNESCO, and UNEP-WCMC, voluntary exclusion zones in most sensitive areas (UNESCO World Heritage sites, IUCN Category Ia/Ib), specific initiatives including artificial nesting sites and seaweed restoration, and biodiversity compensation and net gain plans where regulatory requirements apply.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Galp has identified 139 operational sites (2,362 hectares) owned, leased, or managed in or near protected areas or key biodiversity areas. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Helleniq operates 68 photovoltaic and wind power plants, several of which are located within or near biodiversity-sensitive areas including the Special Protection Area (SPA) for Poultry (part of the Natura 2000 network), Agios Nikolaos Wildlife Sanctuary, forest lands, and Important Bird Areas (IBA) like 'Southern Evros Forest Complex' that host endangered species. The group is also developing additional renewable energy projects in similar sensitive locations, including areas in Cyprus with vulnerable species habitats. To minimize adverse impacts, Helleniq has implemented: conducting environmental impact assessments (EIAs) in accordance with EU Directives 2009/147/EC and 92/43/EEC; specific mitigation measures such as bird avoidance and collision prevention mechanisms on all wind turbines, regular monitoring and removal of dead animals to prevent attracting scavengers, and designing photovoltaic plant fences with 10-15 cm ground clearance to allow animal movement; applying a mitigation hierarchy prioritizing avoidance through careful site selection and minimizing impacts when avoidance is not feasible; conducting continuous environmental monitoring including marine ecosystem assessments; and engaging stakeholder consultations. The company concluded that no material negative impacts on biodiversity and ecosystems have been identified during the reporting period.

evidence.text: HELLENIQ ENERGY operates a total of 68 photovoltaic and wind plants, some of which are located within or near biodiversity-sensitive areas. per_company.ground_truth_answer: MOL Group operates 247 operational sites in or near protected areas (223 km² total area), with the largest concentration in Upstream activities affecting 55 sites covering 204.8 km². per_company.ground_truth_answer: Motoroil operates 24 operational sites located near protected areas, covering 780.69 hectares. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Vopak has not identified ESRS E4 Biodiversity as double material following its IRO screening under ESRS 2 IRO-1, concluding that its operations and value chain do not significantly intersect with biodiversity or ecosystem services. Nevertheless, the company voluntarily discloses biodiversity-related information. Approximately 80% of Vopak's terminals are located within 8 miles (12.5 km) of areas rich in biodiversity, a threshold established through a 2011 study conducted with the University of Wageningen that demonstrated significant potential impacts (NOx depositions, sound and light disturbances) at a distance of five miles from terminals. Vopak identifies biodiversity-sensitive areas using multiple frameworks: IUCN Red List of threatened species, IUCN protected area management categories, Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs), Natura 2000 sites (Europe), UNESCO Man and the Biosphere Program areas, BirdLife International designated areas, and Ramsar Convention wetlands. However, the report does not list specific terminal names or locations that fall within these biodiversity-sensitive designations. To avoid and minimize adverse impacts, Vopak applies mitigation measures across four terminal lifecycle phases: (1) Identification/selection phase — assessing impacts on bird migrations, endangered species, and sound contours, with alternative location design (e.g., relocating jetties); (2) Execution/commissioning phase — relocating endangered species when present and constructing compensatory habitat areas; (3) Operation phase — installing groundwater protection to prevent contaminated flow toward sensitive areas, adapting terminal lighting to minimize bird migration disturbances, controlling NOx/SOx depositions with de-NOx/de-SOx installations where needed, emission control and spill prevention; (4) Demolition phase — avoiding loud construction work during breeding seasons. Specific examples include designing the Panama terminal jetty to prevent disturbance to a coral reef, and planting 30,000 mangrove trees at Tanjung Surat, Pengerang Johor (Malaysia). Vopak updated its Global EIA standard in 2023 to include more detailed biodiversity aspects and intends to use the Integrated Biodiversity Assessment Tool (IBAT) to establish ecological impact KPIs for high-ranking terminals. The company is committed to transitioning from a 'do no harm' to a 'protect, reserve, and restore' approach.

evidence.text: In our assessment, we follow a general 'rule of thumb': terminals within 8 miles (12.5 km) of areas rich in biodiversity may significantly influence the local ecosystem. As approximately 80% of Vopak terminals fall within this range, we acknowledge a shared responsibility to proactively preserve biodiversity.

evidence.text: For each project, the specific effects on biodiversity are addressed to minimize and mitigate the impact by looking for alternative locations (e.g., location of jetties) or environmental compensation. Environmental compensation is deemed a viable option only if all other alternatives fail to result in the required reduction. If terminals are located in the direct vicinity of areas of ecological diversity, extra care is taken to prevent damage to the neighboring area through air, soil, groundwater, and surface water contamination.

evidence.text: Measures taken include installing groundwater protection to prevent contaminated groundwater from flowing towards these areas and adapting the lighting of our terminals to minimize the disturbances for bird migrations. For new terminals, biodiversity matters are taken into account in the design phase of every new terminal through our global standard on Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). For example, the jetty at Vopak's Panama terminal was designed to prevent disturbance to a small coral reef.

Our operations and value chain do not significantly intersect with biodiversity or ecosystem services in a way that creates substantial impacts, dependencies, risks, or opportunities. Hence, ESRS E4 Biodiversity is considered not double material for Vopak.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Vopak provides a substantive voluntary disclosure despite classifying E4 Biodiversity as not double material. The company identifies that approximately 80% of terminals are within 8 miles of biodiversity-rich areas and lists seven categories of biodiversity-sensitive area frameworks used for identification (IUCN, KBA, Natura 2000, Ramsar, UNESCO, BirdLife). It details a comprehensive four-phase lifecycle mitigation approach with concrete examples (Panama jetty design, adapted lighting, groundwater protection, breeding season avoidance). However, fulfillment is Medium rather than High because: (1) the report does not identify specific terminal names or locations within particular biodiversity-sensitive designations as required by E4-5; (2) no quantitative biodiversity metrics or KPIs are provided (only planned through future IBAT analysis); (3) E4 was assessed as immaterial, limiting the depth and specificity of disclosure; and (4) the 80% figure uses a broad 12.5 km radius rather than the proximity thresholds typically expected under ESRS E4-5.

questions.question: What policies and engagement processes does the undertaking have in place to identify and address negative impacts on workers in its value chain, including regarding forced labor and child labor?

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Aker BP has established comprehensive policies and engagement processes to identify and address negative impacts on workers in its value chain, including forced labor and child labor. The company's main governance tools are its Code of Conduct and Human Rights Policy, which explicitly oppose forced labor, human trafficking, and child labor. These policies apply to all employees, non-employees, suppliers, contractors, and business partners. Aker BP implements a risk-based human rights due diligence process aligned with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, OECD Guidelines, and the Norwegian Transparency Act. Engagement mechanisms include: (1) the Business Partner Integrity Procedure, which all suppliers must follow before establishing business relationships; (2) a mandatory Supplier Declaration requiring commitment to responsible operations and adverse impact mitigation; (3) human rights audits of selected suppliers with worker interviews and stakeholder engagement; (4) contractual obligations specifying ethics and compliance requirements; (5) an Integrity Channel for workers to raise concerns; (6) performance review meetings with key suppliers; and (7) safety representatives and site managers who communicate directly with value chain workers. In 2024, Aker BP conducted 7 on-site audits at 10 production sites across 7 countries, encompassing more than 400 workers. Audits had a dedicated focus on human rights (child, forced or compulsory labour), working conditions, health and safety, and violence and harassment. The company updated its Integrity Due Diligence (IDD) process to require suppliers to confirm they have policies and procedures to avoid and manage adverse impacts.

evidence.text: Our code of conduct and human rights policy addresses material topics such as working conditions, human rights (including child, forced and compulsory labour), violence and harassment, and health and safety.
evidence.source_section_header: 8.1 POLICIES AND PROCEDURES

evidence.text: Before establishing or amending any business relationship, we must follow Aker BP's business partner integrity procedure to assess legal and ethical risks and include contractual obligations on ethics and compliance where applicable. This process pays special attention to material topics for value chain workers. To clearly communicate our expectations to our business partners and monitor their compliance where necessary. Requirements are specified in contracts and Aker BP's supplier declaration, which all new suppliers are required to sign prior to becoming an Aker BP supplier.
evidence.source_section_header: 8.1 POLICIES AND PROCEDURES

evidence.text: We conduct audits of a selection of our suppliers and business partners to verify that they comply with applicable laws and regulations, Aker BP's code of conduct, contractual obligations and our supplier declarations, as well as the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work and OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. Worker interviews play a key role in our on-site audits, giving us a unique insight into their views and perspectives. During this year, seven on-site audits were conducted at 10 production sites across seven countries in Europe and Asia, encompassing more than 400 workers. The on-site audits had a dedicated focus towards the following topics: Human rights (child, forced or compulsory labour), Working conditions, Health and safety, Violence and harassment.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: BASF has established comprehensive policies and engagement processes to identify and address negative impacts on workers in its value chain. The company's Supplier Code of Conduct covers forced labor, child labor, human trafficking, labor and social standards, and anti-discrimination guidelines. The BASF Policy Statement on Human Rights further details the company's commitment. BASF conducts supply chain-specific due diligence through a multi-layered approach: suppliers are evaluated using EcoVadis sustainability ratings and Together for Sustainability (TfS) on-site audits. In 2024, 118 raw materials supplier sites were audited and 328 suppliers received EcoVadis assessments. The company uses targeted checks on suppliers in higher-risk countries to prevent child labor risks, such as in the Indian seed business supply chain. Engagement processes include uniform global grievance mechanisms via the Compliance Hotline, available to both employees and external stakeholders including supply chain workers. BASF participates in multi-stakeholder initiatives including WISH (Wage Improvements in Seed Hybrids) addressing child labor in Indian vegetable seeds, and the Responsible Mica Initiative (RMI) advocating for eradication of child labor in India's mica supply chain. When violations are identified through audits or other sources, BASF requires corrective measures and reserves the right to impose commercial sanctions up to termination of business relationships.

evidence.text: Our expectations of our suppliers are laid down in the global Supplier Code of Conduct. Topics covered by the Code of Conduct include compliance with human rights, the exclusion of child labor, forced labor and human trafficking, safeguarding labor and social standards, and antidiscrimination and anticorruption guidelines.

Suppliers are selected, and both new and existing suppliers are evaluated, on the basis both of economic criteria and in particular of ESG standards. Supplier assessment is mainly performed as part of the TfS initiative, of which BASF is a founding member. A total of 118 raw materials supplier sites were audited in relation to sustainability standards on our behalf in 2024. We received EcoVadis sustainability assessments for 328 suppliers with potential sustainability risks. We use targeted checks on suppliers in higher-risk countries to prevent the risk of potential child labor.
evidence.source_section_header: S2-2 / Assessing and growing our suppliers

evidence.text: We promote a culture in which critical issues and concerns can always be raised openly. To do this, we offer uniform grievance mechanisms at the operational level throughout the world. The key tool is our Compliance Hotline. The compliance hotline offers a way of reporting concerns, risks and violations occurring in BASF's activities or in the value chain in confidence and also anonymously. This also includes potential concerns in relation to health and occupational safety as well as child labor. The hotline is available both to BASF employees and to all external stakeholders, and in particular to workers in our supply chains.

Concrete metrics, corrective action procedures, and commercial sanctions for violations demonstrate systematic implementation.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Eni has established comprehensive policies and engagement processes to identify and address negative impacts on workers in its value chain regarding forced labor and child labor. The ECG Policy Respect for Human Rights explicitly rejects forced or compulsory labor (including trafficking, restriction of freedom of movement, seizure of identity documents, labor exploitation, and modern slavery) and child labor in all its worst forms. The Supplier Code of Conduct sets expectations for all business partners. For engagement processes, Eni coordinates worker engagement through its central procurement function, conducting workshops and training on human rights at every stage of supplier interaction (qualification, sourcing, contract execution). Eni implements a risk-based supplier assessment model classifying suppliers by country risk (using Maplecroft data) and activity risk, with controls inspired by SA8000 international standards. In 2024, more than 1,000 human rights audits were carried out on both documents and contractor/subcontractor sites, more than double the 2023 figure. Suppliers with deficiencies are limited from participating in tenders and corrective action plans are agreed upon. In serious cases of non-compliance, supplier relationships are terminated and vendors are excluded from Eni's vendor list. Eni provides whistleblowing mechanisms and expects suppliers to make available their own grievance channels. Human rights are monitored by the Board of Directors, and management incentives are linked to human rights performance.

evidence.text: The Policy also outlines the commitment to respect the minimum age of access to employment, and the measures outlined by applicable international and national legislation on child labour, including its worst forms, as well as the rejection of any form of forced or compulsory labour, including any practice of labour exploitation, such as human trafficking, restriction of freedom of movement and seizure of identity documents.

Equinor conducts risk-based on-site supplier assessments with external human rights experts that specifically assess for forced labour indicators according to the 11 ILO Forced Labour Indicators, including recruitment fees, retention of identity papers, and lack of freedom of movement. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Eni provides grievance mechanisms for affected communities to raise grievances through multiple channels: online (dedicated email addresses and institutional websites), physical submission at administrative/operational headquarters, and collection boxes in project areas. Engagement occurs via public hearings, information sessions, focus groups, and periodic communications throughout the project cycle. Grievances are managed by subsidiaries and tracked in the Stakeholder Management System, with responsibility placed on operational teams to analyse and agree on solutions with claimants. The company prohibits retaliation and ensures confidentiality. For relocation cases, Eni holds dedicated transparent meetings with communities, including vulnerable populations. Grievance outcomes are discussed with applicants, with escalation procedures available for unresolved cases, and quarterly reviews of grievance indicators are conducted to assess mechanism effectiveness.

evidence.text: Eni and its subsidiaries therefore carry out specific consultations with local communities, including indigenous peoples and vulnerable groups; in particular, in the event of economic or physical relocation of communities, dedicated meetings are held in order to inform the communities in a transparent and comprehensive manner, with particular attention to the most vulnerable people. For each new business development initiative, engagement occurs through public hearings open to local communities (unless in contrast with the Country's regulations) and local representatives and in any case ensuring the active participation of authorities (including indigenous people) and local representatives to provide accurate information on business developments and to include any feedback throughout the project cycle.
evidence.source_section_header: COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT

evidence.text: Among the various channels, Eni has defined and applies guiding principles for "Grievance Mechanisms" management whose responsibility, at the operational level, is placed on all the subsidiaries and the districts who analyse and agree on the solution with the claimants (individuals or communities). Any request or complaint received is managed and monitored until closure through agreements with the parties involved, providing a response even if they are not related to Eni's activities. Grievances can be transmitted through online channels, including dedicated email addresses and institutional websites of local companies, or physically at the administrative/operational headquarters or through collection boxes located in areas where the project is held.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Equinor provides multiple grievance mechanisms for affected communities to raise concerns. The company establishes community-based grievance mechanisms (CGMs) for its projects when applicable, which are designed to be prompt, consistent, respectful, simple, local, culturally appropriate, free, well-publicized, and without retribution. Equinor's Human Rights Policy explicitly states it does not tolerate recrimination or retaliation against those who raise concerns in good faith.

evidence.text: Risk-based community grievance mechanisms are set up for our projects when applicable and are built to accommodate specific needs related to the project and community involved. The processes are aligned with all regulations and instruments, including: ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 14001:2015 standards regarding requirements for stakeholder management, the AA1000 Stakeholder Engagement Standard (2015), and IPIECA's 'Community grievance mechanisms in the oil and gas industry' standard.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Motoroil Group maintains open and accessible communication channels with affected communities through multiple established processes. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Neste provides multiple mechanisms for affected communities and workers to raise grievances and engages with indigenous peoples through its human rights due diligence processes. evidence.text: Neste takes a proactive approach in identifying affected and potentially affected stakeholders, and the best ways to engage with them or their legitimate representatives, paying special attention to individuals and groups who may be particularly vulnerable to adverse impacts. per_company.ground_truth_answer: OMV engages with affected communities, including indigenous peoples, through multiple mechanisms: (1) Community Grievance Mechanisms (CGMs) developed in line with UN Guiding Principles, available at operational sites to enable reporting of grievances and resolution of issues, with response times from 24 hours for urgent cases to 45 days for investigations; (2) Social Impact Assessments (SIAs) conducted with free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) from local stakeholders in accordance with IFC Performance Standard 7 and ILO Convention 169; (3) Stakeholder engagement activities including public consultations, meetings, projects, and partnerships to maintain open communication; (4) The Sustainability Directive which outlines requirements for community relations and development managed by the Community Relations and Development function; (5) Specific awareness of indigenous communities near operations in New Zealand (Maui, Pohokura, Maari) and Yemen (Arma district). OMV explicitly commits to respecting communities' civil and political rights, creating business opportunities for local populations, and addressing impacts including disturbance of cultural heritage and involuntary settlements through its Code of Conduct and Human Rights Policy Statement.

evidence.text: We engage with communities, including indigenous communities, through stakeholder engagement activities, public consultations, meetings, projects and partnerships, and community grievance channels to maintain open and transparent communication. This commitment to respecting and incorporating their feedback into our strategic planning and business model helps us align our operations with the values and needs of these communities, supporting sustainable development and enhancing our social license to operate.
